topics.name: too ... to, enough to, so ... that
Adjective + preposition (tired of, afraid of, famous for)
Clauses and linking words in complex sentences

options: The horse was too big to go through the gate.
The horse was too big for go through the gate.
The horse was too big that go through the gate.
questions.rule: The pattern is too + adjective + to + verb: too big to go.

options: The Greeks were tired of the long war.
The Greeks were tired on the long war.
The Greeks were tired at the long war.
questions.rule: When you have had enough of something, you are tired of it.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: The pair is so ... that: so high that no enemy could climb them.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: After a preposition (fond of), a verb takes the -ing form: fond of reading.
We are famous for something we are known for.
enough comes after the adjective: big enough to hold.
too narrow for + noun shows that something is more than the limit.

chat: Why did the Trojans open their gates?
options: They were tired of staying inside the walls.
They were tired of stay inside the walls.
They were tired on staying inside the walls.
questions.rule: tired of + -ing form: tired of staying.

chat: Could the Trojans have saved their city?
options: Yes, if they listen to the priest, they would have saved it.
Yes, if they had listened to the priest, they will save it.
Yes, if they had listened to the priest, they would have saved it.
questions.rule: Third conditional: if + had + past participle, would have + past participle.

questions.source: The horse was so big that it could not go through the gate.
options: The horse was too big to not go through the gate.
The horse was too big to go through the gate.
The horse was too big that it go through the gate.
questions.rule: too ... to already has a negative meaning, so drop 'not': too big to go.

options: Homer was a blind poet which wandered from city to city.
Homer was a blind poet who he wandered from city to city.
Homer was a blind poet who wandered from city to city.
questions.rule: For a person, the adjective clause starts with who, and 'who' is its subject (no extra 'he').

options: If the Trojans had burnt the horse, the Greeks would have fail.
If the Trojans would have burnt the horse, the Greeks would have failed.
If the Trojans had burnt the horse, the Greeks would have failed.
questions.rule: No 'would' in the if-clause. Use had burnt ... would have failed.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: 'That day' and 'were' are past, so the 'that' clause is also past: paid.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: A hero is a person, and here he is the object of 'defeat', so use whom (or who/that).
We say delighted at (or with) the news, not 'to' or 'on'.

questions.rule: The result of an unreal past is might/would have + past participle.

questions.prompt: Make a sentence with an adjective clause.

chat: Can your little brother read The Iliad?
options: No, he is too young to understand it.
No, he is too young that he understands it.
No, he is not enough old to understand it.
questions.rule: Use too young to, or 'not old enough to'. 'enough' goes after the adjective.

questions.source: The wall was so broad that people could walk on it.
options: The wall was broad enough for people to walk on.
The wall was enough broad for people to walk on.
The wall was broad enough that people to walk on.
questions.rule: Adjective + enough + for someone + to + verb: broad enough for people to walk on.

questions.source: Troy was a rich city. It stood near the sea.
options: Troy was a rich city which it stood near the sea.
Troy was a rich city who stood near the sea.
Troy was a rich city which stood near the sea.
questions.rule: which replaces 'It', so 'it' is dropped. Use 'which' for a place or thing.

options: Menelaus was angry on Paris for taking Helen away.
Menelaus was angry with Paris for take Helen away.
Menelaus was angry with Paris for taking Helen away.
questions.rule: We are angry with a person, and after 'for' we use the -ing form: for taking.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has the correct noun clause?
options: The Trojans wondered how had the horse been built.
The Trojans wondered how the horse had been built.
The Trojans wondered how the horse had been build.
questions.rule: A noun clause uses statement order (subject before helper): how the horse had been built.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: After would not have, use the past participle: burnt down (or burned).

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: After to in 'too ... to', use the base form: to lift.

questions.after: far away that nobody could see them.
questions.rule: Adjective/adverb + 'that' clause: so far away that. 'such' needs a noun; 'too' takes 'to'.
If + had + past participle, would have + past participle.

chat: Do you know who built the wooden horse?
options: Yes, a skilful engineer, which knew its secret door.
Yes, a skilful engineer who knew its secret door.
Yes, a skilful engineer who he knew its secret door.
questions.rule: An engineer is a person, so use who; 'who' is the subject, so no extra 'he'.

options: He was afraid of hurting his ankle again.
He was afraid for hurt his ankle again.
He was afraid of hurt his ankle again.
questions.rule: afraid of + -ing form: afraid of hurting.

questions.source: The Trojans broke the wall. So the Greeks got inside.
options: If the Trojans did not break the wall, the Greeks would not have got inside.
If the Trojans had not broke the wall, the Greeks would not have got inside.
If the Trojans had not broken the wall, the Greeks would not have got inside.
questions.rule: Turn the past fact into its opposite: had not broken ..., would not have got ...

options: The priest was too wise to be fooled by the trick.
The priest was too wise to be fool by the trick.
The priest was too wise for be fooled by the trick.
questions.rule: too ... to + passive infinitive: to be fooled (be + past participle).

questions.rule: The main verb of 'The Greek' must be past like the clause: pretended.

questions.before: Hector was not only brave but also capable
questions.rule: We say capable of + -ing form.
A yes/no doubt becomes a noun clause with whether (or if).
so + adjective + that + result clause.

chat: You missed the school bus again!
options: Sorry, if I had woken up early, I would have caught it.
Sorry, if I wake up early, I would have caught it.
Sorry, if I had woken up early, I will catch it.
questions.rule: Regret about the past: if I had woken ..., I would have caught ...

chat: Are you ready for the history quiz on Troy?
options: Yes, I'm quite good at remembering names and dates.
Yes, I'm quite good on remembering names and dates.
Yes, I'm quite good at remember names and dates.
questions.rule: good at + -ing form: good at remembering.

questions.source: The gates were too narrow for the horse to pass through.
options: The gates were so narrow that the horse can not pass through them.
The gates were so narrow that the horse could not pass through them.
The gates were so narrow that the horse could pass through them.
questions.rule: too ... to becomes so ... that ... could not (past, negative).

questions.rule: famous for + -ing form: planning. An earlier past action after 'believed': had left.

options: It is believed that Homer, who lived long ago, have composed both epics.
It is believed that Homer, which lived long ago, composed both epics.
It is believed that Homer, who lived long ago, composed both epics.
questions.rule: The subject of the noun clause is Homer (one person, past): composed. A person takes who.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Before an adjective alone, use so ... that. 'such' needs a noun (such a strong wall).

questions.before: Had Achilles' heel been protected, the arrow
questions.rule: 'Had ... been protected' = 'If ... had been protected', so the result is would not have killed.

questions.prompt: Make a sentence with a noun clause.
questions.rule: why their enemies had left a horse is a noun clause (object of 'wondered') in statement order.

chat: Did you finish the Troy project?
options: No, it was too long that I couldn't finish it in one day.
No, it was so long that I couldn't finish it in one day.
No, it was such long that I couldn't finish it in one day.
questions.rule: Adjective + result clause: so long that. 'too' pairs with 'to'; 'such' needs a noun.

questions.source: If the Trojans had listened to the priest, Troy would have survived.
options: Had the Trojans listened to the priest, Troy would survived.
Had the Trojans had listened to the priest, Troy would have survived.
Had the Trojans listened to the priest, Troy would have survived.
questions.rule: Drop 'If' and put Had before the subject: Had the Trojans listened ..., ... would have survived.

questions.source: The Trojans were too careless to notice the trick.
options: The Trojans were not careful enough to notice the trick.
The Trojans were not enough careful to notice the trick.
The Trojans were not careful enough that noticed the trick.
questions.rule: Use the opposite adjective + enough: too careless = not careful enough to notice.

questions.source: The fleet returned. The Greek gave the signal.
options: When the fleet returned, the Greek gave the signal.
When the fleet returned, then the Greek gave the signal.
When the fleet had returned, so the Greek gave the signal.
questions.rule: When starts the subordinate clause; the main clause needs no 'then' or 'so'.
